title: H6 - Millers enzyme inactivation without steam

market_scan.market_size_text: The addressable frame is the global flour milling industry: ~285 Mt of wheat/meslin flour consumed in 2024 (~$150-190B value, growing ~1-2%/yr), ~450 Mt total flour including other grains. Enzyme inactivation (stabilization) is relevant mainly to whole-grain flour, bran, germ, oats and rice bran - a niche of the ~$12B/yr milling-equipment market, but growing with whole-grain and clean-label demand (~6% CAGR in wheat germ flour). The equipment niche itself is likely a few hundred M$/yr globally, order of magnitude.

regions.Europe: ~EUR 15-20B flour milling turnover (EU-27); ~35 Mt flour/yr; ~25% of world flour consumption
regions.Asia: largest region, ~45% of world flour consumption; China ~60-65 Mt flour (2,000+ mills), India very large but mostly small chakki mills; ~$60-80B flour value
regions.America: ~12% of world flour consumption; US ~20-21 Mt flour, highly consolidated; ~$25-35B flour value incl. LatAm
regions.Africa: ~15% of world flour consumption, fastest growth; mix of large industrial mills (Egypt, Nigeria) and small mills; ~$20-30B flour value

market_scan.target_customers_text: Very fragmented globally but easy to segment. Europe has >3,000 mills (mostly SMEs) reachable via the European Flour Millers association and national bodies; the US is extremely consolidated (~160 wheat mills, top 21 companies = 96% capacity) so a handful of groups (Ardent, ADM, Mennel...) unlock the market; China has 2,000+ mills incl. ~300 large modern plants; India has ~29,000 mostly small chakki mills, hard to reach. Realistic buyers are millers making whole-grain flour, stabilized bran/germ, and oat/rice millers - roughly 10-20% of mills care about stabilization today.

Large: ~500-1,000 large industrial mills worldwide (e.g. China ~300 large plants; US top ~160 mills; European groups)
~60-70% of world flour volume; near-total share in US (96% via top 21 cos.)
Medium: ~2,000-4,000 mid-size mills (bulk of EU-27's >3,000, Turkey ~680, Mexico ~1,100)
Small: ~30,000+ small/chakki mills, concentrated in India (~29k) and Africa
~10-15% of volume; low willingness/ability to pay

market_scan.players_text: Supplier side is split between a few dominant milling OEMs and niche thermal specialists. Bühler dominates hydrothermal stabilization (Granotherm kiln) with Satake, Alapala, Ocrim, Streckel & Schrader offering similar steam/kiln systems. Rice-bran stabilization in Asia is dominated by dry-extrusion suppliers (Insta-Pro, Clextral, local Indian/Chinese OEMs). Dedicated industrial-microwave suppliers (SAIREM, Pueschner, Chinese tunnel makers) exist but offer almost no milling-specific enzyme-inactivation product - the steam-free electric niche is essentially open.
players: Steam/hydrothermal kilns and stabilization lines integrated in new mills (Granotherm DNCB, oat kilners)
Medium (Revtech, Streckel & Schrader, Clextral/Insta-Pro/Wenger extrusion, Vomm)
Specialist continuous stabilizers (vibratory towers, kilns) and dry extruders/expanders for bran/oilseed stabilization
Small (SAIREM, Pueschner, AMTek, Chinese microwave OEMs)
Generic industrial microwave/dielectric heating equipment, mostly dryers and tempering - little enzyme-inactivation-specific product for mills
regulation: ATEX Directive 2014/34/EU + ATEX workplace Directive 1999/92/EC (UK: DSEAR)

Flour/bran dust creates Zone 20-22 explosive atmospheres inside mills; any electric/microwave machine installed in a milling line must be ATEX-certified or placed outside zoned areas - adds design cost and is a real barrier for a small new OEM.
Thermal treatment used as a process control must be validated and monitored; a microwave line needs documented uniform enzyme-inactivation (peroxidase often used as marker) across the product bed.
Microwave generators run at 2,450 MHz ISM band; leakage and EMC limits apply; standard CE-marking burden.
Microwave-treated bran/germ is not considered novel (heating is a conventional process), so no market-authorization hurdle for the treated ingredient.
Energy/decarbonization policy (EU ETS, national electrification incentives)

Electrification of industrial heat is subsidized/favored vs. gas-fired steam boilers - tailwind for an all-electric machine, though EU industrial electricity prices (~0.10-0.15 EUR/kWh vs gas ~0.03-0.05 EUR/kWh) hurt OPEX parity.
Product-contact surfaces must be compliant stainless/food-grade - same burden as incumbents, no extra hurdle.

technologies.name: Direct-steam hydrothermal treatment (status quo)
technologies.how: Saturated steam (100-120 C, ~1-3 bar) injected onto bran/germ/grain in a screw conveyor, kiln or vibratory tower, followed by re-drying and cooling. Sold as kilns (Buehler Granotherm, Streckel & Schrader) or continuous stabilizers (Revtech).
technologies.performance: >95% lipase inactivation with atmospheric steaming, complete peroxidase inactivation; grain steaming 180 s inactivates lipase/peroxidase/xylanase without starch gelatinization; gives 6-18 months shelf life (Glanbia cites 18 months on oat flour).
technologies.limits: Requires boiler, water treatment, steam distribution, condensate handling AND a re-drying step - high capex and floor space; uneconomic for small/medium mills; this is exactly the infrastructure the hypothesis removes.

technologies.name: Dry extrusion / expander cooking
technologies.how: Single-screw extruder uses friction + pressure to hit 120-140 C in seconds, no boiler; dominant method for rice bran stabilization in Asia and oilseeds.
technologies.performance: Best-in-class enzyme kill: residual lipase and LOX <5% of fresh wheat germ in a 2023 LWT comparison; rice-bran FFA kept low for months; ~400 kg/h low-cost units, specific energy ~0.06-0.07 kWh/kg.
technologies.limits: Severe mechanical treatment changes texture/functionality (fine for feed/oil bran, problematic for premium food-grade germ or functional flour); high screw wear; high shear not always wanted in a flour line.

technologies.name: Dry heat: fluid bed, oven/roasting, infrared
technologies.how: Hot air or IR heats product at 130-160 C for minutes; vibrated fluidized bed (VFB) is the gentlest variant.
technologies.performance: 160 C oven heating ranks second to steaming for LOX inactivation; VFB gave the best lipid stability and tocopherol retention in comparative studies.
technologies.limits: Dry heat transfers poorly into particles - longer residence times and less complete lipase inactivation than moist heat; still needs a heat source and doesn't remove the 'why not just use steam' question unless electrified.

technologies.name: Steam explosion (batch)
technologies.how: Bran rehydrated, pressurized at 0.8 MPa / 170 C for ~5 min, then explosively depressurized.
technologies.performance: Inactivates lipase and peroxidase fully; improves soluble fibre and antioxidant extraction vs. autoclaving.
technologies.limits: Batch, high-pressure vessel, needs boiler anyway - opposite of the retrofit-electric value proposition.

technologies.name: Continuous microwave (the hypothesis)
technologies.how: 2.45 GHz volumetric dielectric heating raises product to 60-100+ C in minutes while simultaneously drying (lower water activity adds microbial and enzymatic stability). Lab/pilot studies on wheat germ and bran exist; continuous tunnel equipment is generic (SAIREM, Pueschner, Chinese OEMs).
technologies.performance: 3-4 kW, ~8 min continuous microwave cut wheat-germ residual lipase to ~14-17% and fully inactivated LOX, with good flavor/color; 60-70 C microwave for 5-20 min inactivated lipase with no color/functionality change; combined steam+microwave achieves complete inactivation.
technologies.limits: Lipase is harder to kill than LOX - microwave alone may stall at ~85% inactivation vs. steam's >95%; low-moisture bran is nearly transparent to microwaves (dielectric constant <1.9) so heating efficiency drops as it dries; uniformity at tonne/h scale and ATEX compliance are unproven industrially.

technologies.name: Ohmic heating (emerging)
technologies.how: Electric current passed through moistened bran heats it volumetrically.
technologies.performance: 10-kg batch kept rice-bran FFA at 4.8% after 75 days vs 41.8% untreated.
technologies.limits: Research stage, needs ~30-40% moisture (re-wetting + re-drying), electrodes contact issues - not industrialized.

tech_baseline.why_better_text: An all-electric microwave inactivation unit removes the boiler, steam distribution, water treatment and separate re-dryer that make steam stabilization uneconomic for the thousands of SME mills - it can slot into an existing bran/germ stream as a compact skid with instant on/off and no combustion permits. Microwave heats volumetrically and dries while it inactivates, so the product leaves shelf-stable in one pass, and electrification aligns with EU decarbonization incentives. The honest catch: microwave alone is proven only at lab/pilot scale, lipase is thermally robust, and dry bran absorbs microwaves poorly - a light steam-assist or pre-humidification may still be needed, partially re-importing the complexity being removed.
key_assumptions: Global flour output ~285-450 Mt/yr; whole-grain and stabilized bran/germ streams addressable maybe 5-15% of that (assumed)
Bran is ~20-25% and germ ~2-3% of wheat mass at milling; stabilization applies mainly to these fractions plus oat groats and rice bran (measured)
Steam stabilization line capex (boiler + kiln + dryer) is in the high six to seven figures EUR and only pays at large-mill throughputs >1-2 t/h (assumed)
Microwave wall-to-product efficiency ~50-60%; industrial electricity ~0.10-0.15 EUR/kWh vs gas ~0.03-0.05 EUR/kWh in EU - OPEX parity needs higher energy efficiency or smaller treated mass (assumed)
Target spec: >=90% lipase inactivation and full LOX/peroxidase kill at 0.5-2 t/h continuous, product exit moisture <=12%, ATEX Zone 21/22-compliant execution (assumed)
